Title: Electronic descriptors for designing high-entropy alloy electrocatalysts by leveraging local chemical environments

Electronic descriptors for designing high-
entropy alloy electrocatalysts by leveraging
local chemical environments
Guolin Cao1, Sha Yang1, Ji-Chang Ren
1
& Wei Liu
1,2
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a vast compositional space for ﬁne-tuning
electrocatalytic activities, leveraging millions of distinct active sites on the
surface. However, the intricate local chemical environment poses challenges
to the rational and efﬁcient design of HEA electrocatalysts with high reactivity.
Here, focusing on noble-metal HEAs for oxygen reduction reactions, we pro-
pose a straightforward yet effective descriptor for quantitively determining
the local reactivities of HEAs. This descriptor is based on a linear combination
of the intrinsic d-band ﬁlling of the active center and the neighborhood elec-
tronegativity. Our model offers an accurate and robust description of the
binding strengths of intermediates with different adsorption conﬁgurations
on HEAs, supported by external density functional theory calculations.
Importantly, the local environmental electronegativity of the HEA surface is
strongly related to the d-band proﬁle of the center atom(s) embedded within.
Finally, we establish a library of activity maps for HEAs encompassing nine
noble-metal elements, suggesting that Pd-rich and Ir-rich alloys, such as
Pd–Ag, Ir–Pt, Ir–Au compositions, hold promise as potential candidates for
optimal electrocatalysts.
High entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently emerged as promising can-
didates in heterogeneous catalysis due to their diverse activity sites
and entropy-enhanced stability1–10. In contrast to uniform surfaces that
offer only a limited number of discrete types of adsorptions for reac-
tion intermediates, the complex surface of HEAs, characterized by
randomly distributed multiple principal elements, provides a con-
tinuously tunable range of adsorption energies for intermediates. This
holds promise for designing active sites with “just right” bonding
strengths for key intermediates, adhering to the well-established
Sabatier principle11–14. However, a limited understanding of the rela-
tionship between the intrinsic electronic properties of HEA surface and
reaction intermediates hinders the rational design of HEAs with opti-
mal catalytic performance. Quantum-chemical methods, particularly
density functional theory (DFT), offer a solid foundation for describing
surface reaction processes and enable computer-based design of
complex extended systems15–17. However, characterizing the catalytic
behaviors of diverse local environments requires extensive DFT com-
putations, making research on HEA catalysts challenging. Although
machine learning approaches can accelerate adsorption energy cal-
culations on HEA surfaces, their black-box nature often fails to provide
physical insights for formulating design rules for HEA catalysts18–21.
Descriptor-based methods offer valuable insights by identifying
key electronic features from complex kinetic reaction processes on the
surface22–24. The d-band model25,26 has proven particularly successful in
understanding the binding nature of adsorbates on transition metals.
This model posits that the higher in energy of the d-states, the stronger
the interaction with adsorbate states, attributed to the upper shift of
the anti-bonding states across the Fermi energy15,27–32. Built upon the
Newns-Anderson model33,34, this general principle can be quantita-
tively estimated via a simpliﬁed reactivity descriptor known as the

d-band center (εd), which represents the averaged energy of d-states
projected onto the atom of the active site. Further reﬁnement efforts
have aimed at constructing improved descriptors for noble metals by
extracting additional d-band features of the atom at the active site,
such as d-band ﬁlling (f d) and d-band width (W d)32,35,36. However,
challenges arise when applying these descriptors to alloying surfaces,
resulting in outliers37–39. This discrepancy stems from the reliance on d-
band-based descriptors on local electronic features of the atom at the
active site37–41, which fails to fully consider the effects of the chemical
environment introduced by alloying. This discrepancy is even more
evident in HEAs42, because the diverse chemical environment leads to a
loss of elemental identify43–45, especially a signiﬁcant regulation of the
d-band proﬁle39. Recent theoretical calculations have elucidated that
the regulation of the d-band proﬁles of a metal atom in HEA is closely
linked to charge transfer to/from neighboring atoms, owing to their
unequal electronegativity. Further experimental results have also
highlighted that the substantial difference in electronegativity can
trigger or enhance the local reactivity at electron-enriched sites46–48.
Intuitively, variation in local reactivity across nonuniform sites of HEA
surface depends on the electronic properties of both the metal site
binding with the adsorbate and its local coordination environment.
However, a rigorous formula or relationship between reactivity and the
local chemical environment on the HEA surface, ﬁrmly rooted in solid
theoretical foundations, remains elusive.
In this contribution, we address this challenge by employing high-
throughput DFT calculations on 8170 adsorption systems. We aim to
identify the key features of the active center and its local chemical
environment responsible for determining the binding nature of small
molecules on HEA surfaces. Speciﬁcally, we focus on two crucial
parameters: the ﬁlling fraction of the d-band of the active center
(f Metal
d
) relative to its uniform surface counterpart, and the electro-
negativity (χ) of the reactive domain. We introduce a simple descriptor
(Ω = f Metal
d
+ αχN, as depicted in Fig. 1), which integrates the d-band
proﬁles of the active center (ﬁrst-order response) and the electronic
perturbations from the complex chemical environment (second-order
response). This descriptor effectively predicts the adsorption energies
of small molecular species on noble-metal HEA surfaces, demonstrat-
ing good agreement with DFT calculations. Combined with the ther-
modynamic model, we establish a library of activity maps for HEAs
encompassing nine noble-metal elements that are highly consistent
with available experimental observations. Consequently, our approach
enables rapid screening of HEA catalysts within the vast chemical
space. Remarkably, our model not only establishes a solid foundation
for the coordination environment-regulated d-band proﬁle but also
reveals a fundamental physical framework for comprehending cata-
lytic behaviors on HEA surfaces.

The statistical behaviors of O* adsorbed on HEA surfaces
We illustrate the relationship between the electronic properties of
nonuniform reactive sites and the variations in adsorption energies by
examining the adsorption of oxygen on AgIrPdPtRu HEA surfaces. We
chose noble-metal AgIrPdPtRu systems as a prototype due to their
propensity for forming stable and active solid solutions, which have
recently demonstrated outstanding catalytic performance in oxygen
reduction reactions (ORR)49. We applied averaged lattice constants
from the constituent pure metals for all the HEA systems based on
Vegard’s law50. To further estimate the effect of the variation of the
lattice constants on the adsorption energy, we added +0.3% and −0.3%
changes to the lattice constant of the HEA surfaces. This resulted in a
negligible impact on the values of adsorption energies (Supplementary
Fig. 1). Therefore, in this work, we applied the ﬁxed averaged lattice
constants to generate HEA adsorption systems.

Due to the non-uniformity of the HEA surface, the regulation of
the d-band proﬁle can be separated into two individual character-
istics: (i) the rigid shift of the d-band (Δεd) induced by the charge
transfer between the active center and local-chemical environment;
(ii) the broadening of the d-band (ΔW d) due to the incremental
orbital overlaps between the active center and neighboring atoms, as
depicted in the upper panel of Fig. 2e. Depending on the diverse
regulations governing the d-band proﬁle, the orbital hybridization
between adsorbate and the active center of the HEA surface can be
delineated into two distinct sub-level hybridization diagrams, as
illustrated in Fig. 2e. Diagram-I falls within the purview of Nørskov’s
d-band model, where the value of f d remains constant, and adjust-
ments in the d-band proﬁle entail simultaneously alterations in both
the d-band center ðεdÞ and the d-band width ðW dÞ. These character-
istics jointly dictate the energy level of the anti-bonding states,
thereby inﬂuencing the strength of adsorption. However, with the
consideration of the variation of f d, the correlation between εd and
W d is attenuated. As illustrated in Diagram II, modiﬁcations in the
d-band proﬁle may manifest as adjustable W d alongside invariant εd.
Consequently, this discrepancy leads to varying values of adsorption
energy represented by the same εd, ultimately rendering εd ineffec-
tive as an electronic descriptor for HEA (Fig. 2b). Both types of
hybridization diagrams are additive and concurrently contribute to
the adsorption energy on the HEA surface.

Finally, we incorporated the proposed descriptor with a thermo-

To simulate real adsorption, we initially constructed a 277 Å × 277 Å
HEA surface with the elements randomly distributed. Considering the
linear scaling between OH* and OOH* intermediates of ORR on HEA
surface52, our focus was on the adsorption of the key intermediates O*
and OH*, sufﬁcient for estimating surface reactivity. We achieved co-
adsorptions of these two adsorbates (Supplementary Fig. 4) by
accounting for the neighbor blocking effect53, ensuring the most
probable adsorption network on the HEA surface. Subsequently,
assuming a Sabatier volcano relationship with adsorption energies on
the HEA surface, we computed the microscopic current of each
occupied site using an Arrhenius-like equation49,54,55. Finally, we
obtained the total catalytic reaction current density per site by aver-
aging the various site-microscopic currents over the entire HEA sur-

Discussion
Our developed model provides a comprehensive framework for
understanding reaction activities on noble-metal HEA surfaces,
incorporating the intrinsic ﬁlling fraction of the d-band of the
active center and the electronegativities of the local chemical
environment. The established electronic descriptor effectively
captures the intricate interatomic effects of HEAs on ORR
catalytic performance. We have identiﬁed a robust linear rela-
tionship between the d-band proﬁle of the active center and the
averaged electronegativity of its local chemical environment,
enabling the effective scaling of electronic perturbations by the
electronegativities
of
neighboring
atoms.
This
extends
the
applicability of the d-band model for describing reaction activ-
ities on HEA surfaces. Using the proposed descriptor, we have
generated a library of activity maps for ORR in HEAs, covering Cu,
Ag, Au, and noble-metal elements, and the predicted results are
highly consistent with the experimental reactivity trends of
noble-metal HEAs. Our predictions of high absolute reaction
currents in Pd-rich alloys align well with experimental trends.
Additionally, we have identiﬁed signiﬁcantly larger regions with
optimal activities in compositional space for Ir-rich alloys, such as
Ir–Pt and Ir–Au compositions. These ﬁndings suggest promising
avenues for further exploration in optimizing ORR catalysts using
noble-metal HEAs.
Methods
Density functional theory calculation
All calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation
Package (VASP)58. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with
the revised Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional (RPBE)59 was adopted.
The interaction between the core ion and valence electrons was
described by the projector augmented wave (PAW) method60. The
kinetic energy cutoff was set to 400 eV. A 3 × 3 × 1 supercell with four
layers was considered for all systems. The Monkhorst-Pack grid61 with
3 × 3 × 1 of k-point sampling was utilized, and a vacuum gap of 15 Å was
used to avoid interactions between the periodic slab layers. The geo-
metric relaxation was stopped when the changes in total energy and
forces were smaller than 1 × 10−4 eV and 0.05 eV/Å, respectively. We
conducted a full relaxation of the two uppermost metal layers, allow-
ing the atoms in these layers to adjust their positions until reaching a
state of minimum energy. The metal atoms in the two bottommost
layers were kept ﬁxed at their bulk positions throughout the relaxation
process.

Electronegativity selection
In this work, we selected Linus Pauling’s deﬁnition of atomic
electronegativity62 with modiﬁed values by Allred63. For atoms in
molecules or extended systems, the electronegativities of bonded
atoms can be evaluated in two ways: (i) the chemical potential of the
systems64, which states that electronegativity equalization is required
for all bonded atoms, or so-called Sanderson principle65; (ii) average
electron binding energy of the system, as proposed by Roald Hoff-
mann and the collaborators66, which construct an efﬁcient way for
energy partitioning of the molecules and extended systems. The ﬁrst
method is in line with Mulliken’s deﬁnition of electronegativity,
which is conceptually correct but not suitable for the description of
the non-uniform active sites on HEA surfaces with diverse reactiv-
ities. Here we used the averaged Pauling’s atomic electronegativity of
the local environment on HEA surfaces, which is consistent with
Hoffmann’s energy partitioning theory. As within Hoffmann’s deﬁ-
nition of the average electron binding energy X, the formula is
expressed as:

Check submission. First of all, the dispatcher will check whether the

File uploading and downloading. The uploading ﬁles include four

and downloading have been performed with os and shutil mod-

and stored in JavaScript Object Notation format to the local
device.
Job submission and monitoring. After uploading needed ﬁles, the
dispatcher would generate scripts onto sever for executing DFT cal-
culation tasks with a homemade job scheduling system. Then, the job
monitoring subroutine monitors the “state” of the tasks during the
whole calculation process correct the errors, and resubmit it on-
the-ﬂy.
Co-adsorption model
Firstly, a 277 Å × 277 Å HEA surface was constructed based on the SQS
method. Then, the adsorption energy was predicted for each active
site (on-top site for O* adsorption fcc hollow site for OH* adsorption)
on the HEA surface with our proposed descriptor, and subsequently all
the active sites according to the values of adsorption energy. In this
study, the entire process of the ORR was approximated by evaluating
the adsorption energies of the key intermediates O* and OH*. This
approach assumes that the Brønsted–Evans–Polanyi relationship68 and
linear scaling relations30 between the intermediates still hold (Sup-
plementary Fig. 3). Therefore, only the adsorption energies of O* and
OH* have been calculated and utilized for the subsequent calculations
of reaction currents. The O*/OH* adsorbs step-by-step on the HEA
surface according to the following rule: (i) the starting adsorption site
would be the one with the lowest adsorption energy; (ii) for the O*
adsorbed fcc hollow site, its three neighboring on-top site should
avoid the OH* adsorption, preventing the so-called blocking effect; and
(iii) the adsorption would continue until no more free surface sites
remained.
